items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "transmission"?
options: The number of people with a disease at a particular time in a population.
The passing of a pathogen from one host to another.
The number of new cases of a disease per unit of population in a given time.
Describes a disease that is always present in a population.
items.answer: The passing of a pathogen from one host to another.
items.markingKey: Transmission: the passing of a pathogen from one host to another.

items.stem: Explain why HIV infection leads to AIDS.
items.answer: HIV infects and destroys T helper cells; the immune system can no longer coordinate responses; opportunistic infections such as TB and pneumonia develop.
items.markingKey: HIV infects and destroys T helper cells [1]; the immune system can no longer coordinate responses [1]; opportunistic infections such as TB and pneumonia develop [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why cholera is common after floods or in refugee camps.
items.answer: Sewage contaminates drinking water; overcrowding; lack of clean water and sanitation allow faecal–oral transmission.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Sewage contaminates drinking water; overcrowding; lack of clean water and sanitation allow faecal–oral transmission (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: A health ministry recorded 850 new cases of measles in 2018 and 1,196 in 2022 in a region with a population of 2,500,000 (assume constant). (a) Calculate the incidence per 100 000 people in each year. (b) Calculate the percentage change in incidence.
items.answer: (a) 34 and 47.8 per 100 000 (b) 40.7% (an increase)

items.stem: A health ministry recorded 1,416 new cases of malaria in 2018 and 1,577 in 2022 in a region with a population of 2,500,000 (assume constant). (a) Calculate the incidence per 100 000 people in each year. (b) Calculate the percentage change in incidence. (c) Describe how malaria is transmitted and suggest one reason for the change.
items.answer: (a) 56.6 and 63.1 per 100 000 (b) 11.4% (an increase) (c) Bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes (the vector); also blood transfusion and from mother to fetus. Possible reason for the rise: breakdown of control measures (e.g. use insecticide-treated mosquito nets), drug resistance, migration or conflict.

items.stem: Public-health officials in Cairo are investigating an outbreak of HIV/AIDS. (a) Describe how the disease is transmitted. (b) Suggest two social or economic factors that could increase the spread of the disease.
items.answer: (a) Exchange of body fluids: unprotected sex, sharing needles, infected blood products, mother to child across the placenta, at birth or in breast milk. (b) Overcrowding; poverty / poor sanitation; lack of health care or vaccination; migration / conflict; lack of education.
items.markingKey: (a) any 2 from: Exchange of body fluids: unprotected sex; sharing needles; infected blood products; mother to child across the placenta; at birth or in breast milk (1 mark each) [2] (b) any 2 from: Overcrowding; poverty / poor sanitation; lack of health care or vaccination; migration / conflict; lack of education (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which pathogen causes measles?
items.answer: Measles virus (a morbillivirus)
items.markingKey: Measles: measles virus (a morbillivirus) (virus).

items.stem: Which disease is caused by a protoctist?
items.answer: Malaria
items.markingKey: Plasmodium is a protoctist.

items.stem: Explain why measles is particularly dangerous for malnourished children.
items.answer: Their immune systems are weaker, so complications such as pneumonia, encephalitis and blindness (with vitamin A deficiency) are more likely.
items.markingKey: any 2 from: Their immune systems are weaker; so complications such as pneumonia; encephalitis and blindness (with vitamin A deficiency) are more likely (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: A student in Karachi states: "Malaria is caused by mosquitoes." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Malaria is caused by the protoctist Plasmodium; the mosquito is the vector.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Malaria is caused by the protoctist Plasmodium; the mosquito is the vector. [2]

items.stem: Kenji writes in a revision note: "HIV and AIDS are the same thing." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the syndrome that develops when the immune system is severely damaged.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: HIV is the virus; AIDS is the syndrome that develops when the immune system is severely damaged. [2]

items.stem: A health ministry recorded 1,317 new cases of tuberculosis (TB) in 2020 and 1,132 in 2024 in a region with a population of 250,000 (assume constant). (a) Calculate the incidence per 100 000 people in each year. (b) Calculate the percentage change in incidence.

A health ministry recorded 1,070 new cases of malaria in 2015 and 774 in 2019 in a region with a population of 1,200,000 (assume constant). (a) Calculate the incidence per 100 000 people in each year. (b) Calculate the percentage change in incidence. (c) Describe how malaria is transmitted and suggest one reason for the change.
items.answer: (a) 89.2 and 64.5 per 100 000 (b) −27.7% (a decrease) (c) Bites of infected female Anopheles mosquitoes (the vector); also blood transfusion and from mother to fetus. Possible reason for the fall: better control, e.g. use insecticide-treated mosquito nets.

items.stem: Describe the causes and methods of transmission of cholera, malaria, TB, HIV/AIDS and measles.
items.answer: Cholera: Vibrio cholerae, faecal–oral water/food. Malaria: Plasmodium, Anopheles vector. TB: Mycobacterium, droplets / milk. HIV: virus, body fluids. Measles: virus, droplets.
items.markingKey: one mark per disease [5]; extra detail [2] [7]

items.stem: Public-health officials in Lima are investigating an outbreak of cholera. (a) Name the causative organism and state the type of pathogen. (b) Suggest two social or economic factors that could increase the spread of the disease. (c) Suggest why it is important to identify the pathogen quickly.
items.answer: (a) Vibrio cholerae; bacterium. (b) Overcrowding; poverty / poor sanitation; lack of health care or vaccination; migration / conflict; lack of education. (c) To choose the correct treatment (e.g. antibiotics are useless against viruses) and control measures.
items.markingKey: (a) Vibrio cholerae [1]; bacterium [1] [2] (b) any 2 from: Overcrowding; poverty / poor sanitation; lack of health care or vaccination; migration / conflict; lack of education (1 mark each) [2] (c) To choose the correct treatment (e.g. antibiotics are useless against viruses) and control measures [2] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "isolation of people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease"?
items.answer: Quarantine
items.markingKey: Quarantine: isolation of people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease.

items.stem: Explain why insecticide-treated bed nets reduce the incidence of malaria.
items.answer: Anopheles mosquitoes feed at night; nets stop them biting sleeping people and the insecticide kills them, so fewer transmit Plasmodium.
items.markingKey: Anopheles mosquitoes feed at night [1]; nets stop them biting sleeping people and the insecticide kills them [1]; so fewer transmit Plasmodium [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why measles was eliminated from some countries but has returned.
items.answer: High vaccination coverage gave herd immunity; when coverage fell (e.g. vaccine hesitancy, conflict) the pathogen spread again among unvaccinated people.
items.markingKey: High vaccination coverage gave herd immunity [1]; when coverage fell (e.g. vaccine hesitancy, conflict) the pathogen spread again among unvaccinated people [1] [2]

items.stem: The basic reproduction number (R₀) of rubella is about 6. (a) Calculate the herd immunity threshold using (1 − 1/R₀) × 100. (b) The vaccine is 90% effective. Calculate the vaccination coverage needed to reach the threshold.

The basic reproduction number (R₀) of measles is about 18. (a) Calculate the herd immunity threshold using (1 − 1/R₀) × 100. (b) The vaccine is 93% effective. Calculate the vaccination coverage needed to reach the threshold. (c) Explain how herd immunity protects babies too young to be vaccinated.
items.answer: (a) 94.4% (b) 101.6% – more than 100%, so herd immunity cannot be reached with this vaccine alone (c) Most people around them are immune, so the pathogen cannot spread through the population and is unlikely to reach the baby.
items.markingKey: (a) (1 − 1/18) × 100 = 94.4% [2] (b) 94.4 ÷ 0.93 = 101.6% [2] (c) few susceptible hosts / chain of transmission broken [1]; baby unlikely to meet infected person [1] [6]

items.stem: Health workers are planning a programme to reduce malaria in a flooded district in Sindh. (a) Suggest and explain three measures that could be included. (b) Describe how the success of the programme could be measured.
items.answer: (a) Use insecticide-treated mosquito nets: stop female Anopheles mosquitoes biting at night and kill them, so Plasmodium is not transmitted. Spray insecticides on walls of houses: kills adult mosquitoes that rest on walls after feeding, reducing the vector population. Drain stagnant water where mosquitoes breed: removes breeding sites for mosquito larvae, reducing the number of vectors. (b) Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after, over several years, compared with a similar area.
items.markingKey: (a) three measures, each explained [3] (b) any 2 from: Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after; over several years; compared with a similar area (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which measure is used specifically to control the spread of malaria?
items.answer: Release fish that eat larvae
items.markingKey: Malaria: use insecticide-treated mosquito nets; spray insecticides on walls of houses; drain stagnant water where mosquitoes breed; antimalarial drugs (prophylaxis and treatment); release fish that eat larvae.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "quarantine"?
options: The average number of people infected by one infected person in a population with no immunity.
Drugs that slow the replication of retroviruses such as HIV.
Protection of unvaccinated people in a population when a large enough proportion is immune that the pathogen cannot spread effectively.
Isolation of people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease.
items.answer: Isolation of people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease.
items.markingKey: Quarantine: isolation of people who may have been exposed to an infectious disease.

items.stem: Explain why there is no vaccine yet for HIV.
items.answer: HIV mutates rapidly, changing its antigens; it hides inside T helper cells; it destroys the cells needed for the immune response.
items.markingKey: HIV mutates rapidly, changing its antigens [1]; it hides inside T helper cells [1]; it destroys the cells needed for the immune response [1] [3]

items.stem: Amara writes in a revision note: "Herd immunity requires everyone to be vaccinated." Identify the error and write a correct statement.
items.answer: Herd immunity needs only a large enough proportion of people to be immune.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: Herd immunity needs only a large enough proportion of people to be immune. [2]

Explain how each of these measures helps to control malaria: (i) use insecticide-treated mosquito nets (ii) release fish that eat larvae.
items.answer: (i) Stop female Anopheles mosquitoes biting at night and kill them, so Plasmodium is not transmitted. (ii) Biological control reduces mosquito larvae and so the number of adult vectors.

items.stem: Explain how each of these measures helps to control tuberculosis (TB): (i) contact tracing and isolating infected people (ii) BCG vaccination.
items.answer: (i) Infectious people are found and treated, so they do not spread droplets to others. (ii) Gives immunity (especially to children), so fewer people develop TB and spread it.
items.markingKey: (i) explanation linked to transmission / effect on pathogen or vector [2] (ii) explanation [2] [4]

items.stem: Discuss the biological, social and economic factors that need to be considered in the prevention and control of malaria, cholera, TB, HIV/AIDS and measles.
items.answer: Biological: vectors, pathogen variation, resistance, latent infections, vaccine availability. Social: overcrowding, sanitation, education, cultural practices, conflict. Economic: cost of drugs, nets, water treatment, health workers. Examples of measures for each disease.
items.markingKey: biological factors [2]; social [2]; economic [1]; specific examples [2] [7]

items.answer: (a) Overcrowding, poverty, poor infrastructure (water, sanitation, roads), lack of health workers, conflict, cost of drugs / vaccines, cultural factors. (b) Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after, over several years, compared with a similar area.

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "bacteriostatic"?
options: The passing of genes, often on plasmids, from one bacterium to another, including between species, by conjugation.
The ability of a bacterium to survive exposure to an antibiotic that would normally kill it or stop its growth.
Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a strain of bacteria resistant to many antibiotics.
Describes an antibiotic that stops bacteria growing and dividing.
items.answer: Describes an antibiotic that stops bacteria growing and dividing.
items.markingKey: Bacteriostatic: describes an antibiotic that stops bacteria growing and dividing.

items.stem: Explain how a population of antibiotic-resistant bacteria develops.
items.answer: Random mutation gives a resistance allele; when the antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria die; resistant ones survive and reproduce by binary fission, passing on the allele; plasmids spread it horizontally; over generations most are resistant (natural selection).
items.markingKey: any 4 from: Random mutation gives a resistance allele; when the antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria die; resistant ones survive and reproduce by binary fission, passing on the allele; plasmids spread it horizontally; over generations most are resistant (natural selection) (1 mark each) [4]

items.stem: Explain why patients should finish a course of antibiotics even if they feel better.
items.answer: To kill all bacteria, including those that are less susceptible; stopping early leaves survivors that can multiply and be selected for resistance.
items.markingKey: To kill all bacteria, including those that are less susceptible [1]; stopping early leaves survivors that can multiply and be selected for resistance [1] [2]

Diameter of clear zone / mm, trial 1: 12, 17, 22, 27, 31; trial 2: 12, 17, 21, 26, 31; trial 3: 13, 17, 22, 26, 31. Calculate the mean diameter of clear zone at 32 μg cm⁻³.
items.answer: 31 mm

items.stem: Chloe spread a culture of bacteria evenly on nutrient agar plates and placed paper discs soaked in different concentrations of an antibiotic on them. After 48 hours at 25 °C, the diameter of the clear zone around each disc was measured. Results table. Antibiotic concentration / μg cm⁻³: 10, 25, 50, 100, 200. items.stem: Explain why antibiotic resistance spreads more rapidly in bacteria than resistance in animals.
items.answer: Bacteria reproduce very quickly (short generation time); resistance genes on plasmids can be transferred between bacteria, even different species.

items.stem: Why does the number of resistant bacteria increase when an antibiotic is used frequently?
options: The antibiotic causes mutations for resistance
Bacteria learn to break down the antibiotic
Patients become immune to the antibiotic
The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, so resistant bacteria survive and reproduce
items.answer: The antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria, so resistant bacteria survive and reproduce

items.stem: In a patient in Karachi, 100 antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive a course of antibiotics. The generation time is 40 minutes. (a) Calculate the number of resistant bacteria after 4 hours (assume no deaths). (b) Explain why the population after this time is almost entirely resistant.
items.answer: (a) 6,400 (b) The antibiotic killed susceptible bacteria (selection pressure); only resistant bacteria survived and reproduced, passing on the resistance allele to all their offspring.
items.markingKey: (a) 6 generations [1]; 100 × 2^6 = 6,400 [1] (b) selection by antibiotic [1]; resistant survive and reproduce / pass on allele [1] [4]

items.answer: (a) 83.3% (b) 87.7% (c) Most people around them are immune, so the pathogen cannot spread through the population and is unlikely to reach the baby.

items.stem: Health workers are planning a programme to reduce tuberculosis (TB) in a crowded city district in Lagos. (a) Suggest and explain three measures that could be included. (b) Describe how the success of the programme could be measured.
items.answer: (a) BCG vaccination: gives immunity (especially to children), so fewer people develop TB and spread it. Contact tracing and isolating infected people: infectious people are found and treated, so they do not spread droplets to others. Long courses of several antibiotics (DOTS): kill Mycobacterium completely and reduce the chance of resistance; observed treatment makes sure the course is completed. (b) Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after, over several years, compared with a similar area.
items.markingKey: (a) three measures, each explained [3] (b) any 2 from: Record the number of new cases (incidence) per 100 000 before and after; over several years; compared with a similar area (1 mark each) [2]

items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "antibiotic resistance"?
options: Meticillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus, a strain of bacteria resistant to many antibiotics.
The ability of a bacterium to survive exposure to an antibiotic that would normally kill it or stop its growth.
The passing of genes, often on plasmids, from one bacterium to another, including between species, by conjugation.
An antibiotic that inhibits the enzymes that form cross-links in bacterial cell walls, so bacteria burst by osmosis.
items.answer: The ability of a bacterium to survive exposure to an antibiotic that would normally kill it or stop its growth.
items.markingKey: Antibiotic resistance: the ability of a bacterium to survive exposure to an antibiotic that would normally kill it or stop its growth.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain why patients should finish a course of antibiotics even if they feel better. (b) Explain how a population of antibiotic-resistant bacteria develops.
items.answer: (a) To kill all bacteria, including those that are less susceptible; stopping early leaves survivors that can multiply and be selected for resistance. (b) Random mutation gives a resistance allele; when the antibiotic is used, susceptible bacteria die; resistant ones survive and reproduce by binary fission, passing on the allele; plasmids spread it horizontally; over generations most are resistant (natural selection).

items.stem: In a patient in Lisbon, 10 antibiotic-resistant bacteria survive a course of antibiotics. The generation time is 30 minutes. (a) Calculate the number of resistant bacteria after 8 hours (assume no deaths). (b) Explain why the population after this time is almost entirely resistant.
items.answer: (a) 655,360 (b) The antibiotic killed susceptible bacteria (selection pressure); only resistant bacteria survived and reproduced, passing on the resistance allele to all their offspring.

items.stem: Explain how antibiotics such as penicillin act on bacteria, how resistance develops and spreads, and how its impact can be reduced.
items.answer: Penicillin inhibits cross-linking enzymes → weak wall → osmotic lysis; not effective on viruses / human cells. Resistance: random mutation, selection, survival and reproduction, plasmids, conjugation. Reduction: fewer prescriptions, complete course, narrow-spectrum, hygiene, less in farming, new antibiotics.

items.stem: In a hospital in Dubai, the percentage of Staphylococcus aureus infections caused by MRSA rose from 12% to 40% over ten years. (a) Calculate the percentage increase in the proportion of MRSA infections. (b) Explain how MRSA became common in the hospital.
items.answer: (a) 233% (b) Random mutation gave resistance; heavy antibiotic use killed susceptible bacteria; resistant ones survived, reproduced and spread between patients (natural selection); plasmid transfer.

items.stem: Which cells are infected and destroyed by HIV?
items.answer: T helper lymphocytes

items.stem: Give a reason for each answer. (a) Explain why HIV infection leads to AIDS. (b) Explain why cholera is common after floods or in refugee camps.
items.answer: (a) HIV infects and destroys T helper cells; the immune system can no longer coordinate responses; opportunistic infections such as TB and pneumonia develop. (b) Sewage contaminates drinking water; overcrowding; lack of clean water and sanitation allow faecal–oral transmission.

items.answer: Viruses lack cell walls, ribosomes and metabolism targeted by antibiotics; they reproduce inside host cells.
